I am of the belief that there should only be upvote on voat, or making it so that heavily downvoted posts are not hidden. In practice downvoting is only used when someone is offended by a post. The issue here is that people are often offended by opposition to their own opinions and thus the downvote system often serves to hide dissenting opinions. One could argue that the upvote system already does this because people will tend to agree with people of the same opinion or "circlejerk" their own ideas, and I would agree. However I believe that the ability to downvote posts gives enhances this "circlejerk" and gives people further power to hide dissenting opinions. The best solution to problem in my opinion is to remove the ability to downvote, or by default make it so heavily downvoted posts are not hidden.

Hey, everyone. Is anyone out there interested in conditionals? I am working on indicarive conditionals at the moment, and it would be great to get in touch with someone who's interested in it. So far I've been reading Bennett's classic book on the topic, as well as the obvious papers by Stalnaker, Jackson, Lewis and Edgington. My focus is to understand how issues in probability, assertion and semantics all come together in the mystery of analytic conditionals. So far I have been looking at a recent theory by Anthony Gillies. It would be awesome to have someone to discuss it with.

Of course, I understand not everyone is familiar with the topic, and I wouldn't blame any of you that may have come across it and skipped it over because it seemed arid. But I do encourage you to give it a try. The topic is essentially about how to analyse and explain the way we use the word 'if' as in: 'If I keep going out for midnight snacks I'll go over my budget'. These are very good places to start:

An introductory article by an expert on the topic: http://rci.rutgers.edu/~thony/resources/phil-language-and-indicatives-radio-edit.pdf

A more comprehensive survey article by legendary Dorothy Edgington: http://plato.stanford.edu/entries/conditionals/

A very accessible, clear and nicely put-together course on conditionals, with extensive references: http://www.niu.edu/~gpynn/conditionals.html

While I am not familiar with the topic I am willing to learn about those things you are most interested in for the reason that I know how much it sucks to not have someone to discuss that which you are obsessed with. Is there a particular thought or theory you want to try out?

Hey, thanks for the reply. Don't worry, I do have some people to discuss with, just not as many as I wish I could have. But it's great that you are interested in the topic. The best introduction is probably the Edgington article and the set of lectures I linked to above. I'm afraid it's a bit technical for me to explain right now, but just to stoke some further curiosity in you, consider the following:

It is the case that either not-P is the case or Q is the case, therefore if P is the case, Q is the case.

That seems like a reasonable inference. And yet, as the materials above explain, if that inference is valid, it would imply that the following inference is also valid:

I am not in London. Therefore, if I am in London, I am in Scotland.

Very puzzling! (The articles above explain why the validity of the first commits you to the validity of the second. These are the so-called 'paradoxes of material implication'. I can explain to you why exactly that happens, but I think it's better if I leave you in suspence and you go and find out on your own!)

It was uncommon to me. Talos Principle was really great. It was like a more serious Portal, with a more thoughtful fascinating story. I was obsessed with it while I was playing it, and it really stuck with me for weeks after.

I've also been playing Hand of Fate lately which is a very fascinating deck building, roguelike brawler? Your playing some card game with a wizard, and you build a deck of equipment and a deck of challenges. Then the wizard arrays the challenges in a grid and you move your game piece across it earning rewards and looking for the boss. Many of the encounters are resolved in a brawler game you get sucked into? I haven't gotten very far, but I'm find allusions to the fact that the game and real life might be intertwined, and you are trapped maybe? Or maybe I'm reading too much into the story.

Lastly, it's been getting some press, so it's not entirely unknown, but I played Her Story and I had a really good time. The entire game is just you browsing through a database of police interviews. You don't know the questions, you can't watch them in order, all you can do is type in search terms against the transcripts. But even then, if the search term pulls back 100 videos, you only get to watch the first 5. The game starts off with "MURDER" already entered as the search term and you go from there. Most of the fun is trying to figure out the right search terms to get more information on a clue, or writing down notes about the video timestamps trying to work out the context of the dialog in the videos. The weird thing about the game is there really isn't a beginning middle or end. You just sort of play until you are satisfied that you've figured out the mystery. Or not? There is a lot of debate about what actually happened, and a lot of different story theories, which can be a lot of fun. This is another game that like Talos Principle, really stuck with me after I finished it.

Although I have no more information than you do, what you have said is most likely correct. Whenever a page is loaded, the contents of the page itself like the title and description are most likely being cached. However, the comments section is dynamic and therefore every time someone loads the page that is another request and presumably expensive database operation (depending on the type of query and how your database is configured).

The current method is how I would handle reducing load. Whoever is handling this stuff at Voat is banking on the fact that not everyone will click the continue viewing link therefore potentially saving a few hits to the database. Rather than assuming everyone wants to see every comment, they know only a certain subset of visitors actually will. Reddit limits threads on a submission presumably for this reason, but they have more server resources at their disposal, so the depth they allow is greater than Voat currently does.
